newsitem.title: UK: BSkyB, British Telecom invest $433 million in TV venture.
newsitem.headline: BSkyB, British Telecom invest $433 million in TV venture.

text.p: British Sky Broadcasting Group Plc and British Telecommunications Plc said they teamed up to form a new company Wednesday that will spend $433 million to bring digital interactive television service to Britain next year.

British Sky Broadcasting and British Telecom will each own 32.5 percent of the new company, Midland Bank Plc will own 20 percent and Matsushita Electric Industrial Co. Ltd. of Japan the remaining 15 percent, the companies said.

The partners in the new company, British Interactive Broadcasting Ltd. (BIB), said they plan to spend 265 million pounds ($433 million) to bring the cost of set-top boxes needed for the new service to 200 pounds ($327) or less for consumers.
"Interactive TV will add a new dimension to the broadcasting revolution in Britain and Sky again is at the forefront of these exciting changes," BSkyB Chief Executive Sam Chisholm said.

BSkyB, controlled by Rupert Murdoch's News Corp., had planned to launch digital satellite TV service late this year but has pushed that back to spring 1998. The venture is expected to break even after five years, officials said.

The new service will offer 200 channels of pay per view sports, films and other programmes, home banking, online games and other services. The interactive part of the service is expected to come on stream later next year, officials said.

Industry analysts said it would take time for the interactive segment to catch on. The digital broadcasts will offer viewers better picture and sound quality, more channels and the interactive services.

"The main demand will initially be for movies and sport and BSkyB will take the cream there," one analyst said. "The interactive services are a thing that is very nice to have rather than a must have."
The combination of Britain's leading pay television company and its biggest telephone company is certain to be examined closely by regulators.

"If the joint venture works in a way which doesn't distort the market, the range of services it offers will be good news for customers," said Don Cruickshank, director-general of Oftel, Britain's telecommunications regulator.
Cruickshank said he would examine the venture and its implications for consumers "very closely" but leave a final ruling to European regulators.
BSkyB deputy managing director David Chance said the company had contacted Oftel officials and was confident the new venture would be approved.
British cable operator Telewest Communications, which is planning to start offering digital service later this year, was swift to voice its concerns.

"With respect to BIB, our only concern will be to ensure that a joint venture involving quasi-monopolists does not lead to anti-competitive behaviour. We are sure that the regulatory bodies will share this concern," Telewest Chief Executive Stephen Davidson said.

The venture also ordered 1 million set-top boxes from Matsushita, Grundig/Hyundai, a venture of Grundig of Germany and Hyundai of South Korea, and two British electronics companies, Pace Micro Technology Plc and Amstrad Plc.

BSkyB also said pretax profit rose 15 percent to 81.6 million pounds ($133 million) in its third quarter ended on March 31 from 71.2 million ($116 million) a year earlier. Results for the company, which has 6.2 million subscribers in Britain and Ireland, were in line with analysts' estimates.
BSkyB stock added 7 pence (11 cents) to 602.5 pence ($9.84) on the London Stock Exchange.
